questions.q: What is the main difference between a linter and a static analysis tool?
options: A linter checks style and consistency; static analysis looks for likely bugs and security patterns — neither executes the code
A linter runs the application; static analysis does not
Static analysis only works on compiled languages
There is no real difference; they are the same category of tool
questions.explain: Both read source code without running it, but linting targets style/consistency while static analysis targets patterns likely to be bugs or security problems.

questions.q: In `ruff check src/`, how does the CI job know whether linting passed?
options: ruff always exits 0 regardless of findings
ruff prints 'PASSED' in green text that CI parses
ruff's exit code — non-zero the moment it finds a violation — fails the job, the same gate pattern as a test step
A human reviewer must approve the lint output manually
questions.explain: Like a test command, ruff communicates pass/fail through its process exit code, which the workflow engine checks.

A linter for CSS files only
GitHub's built-in static analysis engine, run as a workflow against pull requests to find bug and security patterns
A replacement for unit testing
questions.explain: CodeQL is GitHub's static analysis engine that scans pull requests for code patterns likely to be bugs or vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Why does Northbridge Retail run linting as its own separate job rather than folding it into the test job?
options: Linting cannot run on the same runner as tests
So a lint failure and a test failure show up as two distinctly-named checks instead of one job failing for an unclear reason
Separate jobs are required by GitHub Actions syntax
It has no real benefit; it's just a stylistic choice
questions.explain: Separating the jobs means each failure is named and visible on its own, making it immediately clear which category of check actually failed.

questions.q: Why can't a 100%-passing test suite guarantee code is free of security problems?
options: 100% coverage is impossible to achieve in practice
Test suites always have bugs themselves
Security problems can only be found by manual code review
Tests only check what they were specifically written to check — a vulnerability in an untested code path won't be caught by passing tests
questions.explain: Tests verify the behaviors someone wrote a test for. Static analysis looks at the shape of the code itself, independent of what any specific test exercises.
